pos: n. (the firstborn son of Manasseh, and the man of war who took Gilead)
etymology: Hebrew Makir (H4353), from makar (H4376), to sell; possibly meaning "sold" or, by extension, "bought," i.e., acquired at a price.
biblical_def: Machir is the firstborn son of Manasseh (Joshua 17:1), and so the grandson of Joseph, remembered first for a tender family detail: “the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph’s knees” (Genesis 50:23). Joseph, dying in Egypt still believing the promise of the land, lived to see his great-grandchildren by Machir’s line. The rest of Machir’s record is martial rather than domestic: “Machir begat Gilead” (Numbers 26:29), and “the children of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead, and took it, and dispossessed the Amorite which was in it” (Numbers 32:39). Because he was, in Joshua’s own summary, “a man of war,” his family alone among the half-tribe of Manasseh received the whole of Gilead and Bashan east of Jordan (Joshua 17:1). Machir is thus both a personal name and, almost immediately in the text, the name of a whole clan and a whole conquered region — “the family of the Machirites” (Numbers 26:29) — the pattern by which a patriarch’s name becomes a tribe’s inheritance. He is not to be confused with the later Machir the son of Ammiel of Lo-debar, a man of a wholly different generation and a wholly different kindness (2 Samuel 9:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Machir; the Hebrew root means to sell or to acquire by purchase, fitting a firstborn son whose descendants themselves acquired, by conquest under divine grant, the land of Gilead.
webster_full: MACHIR, n. The firstborn son of Manasseh, whose descendants conquered and inherited the land of Gilead east of the Jordan.
GILEAD, n. A mountainous region east of the Jordan, balm-producing, given as inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh.
FIRSTBORN, n. The eldest child, entitled by ancient custom and by divine law to a double portion of the inheritance.
INHERIT, v.t. To take by descent from an ancestor; to receive as a possession by gift or right of birth.
CONQUEST, n. The act of overcoming and subduing by force; acquisition by war.
scriptures: Genesis 50:23
And Joseph saw Ephraim's children of the third generation: the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph's knees.
Numbers 26:29
Of the sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the family of the Machirites: and Machir begat Gilead: of Gilead come the family of the Gileadites.
Numbers 32:39
And the children of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead, and took it, and dispossessed the Amorite which was in it.
Joshua 17:1

There was also a lot for the tribe of Manasseh; for he was the firstborn of Joseph; to wit, for Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead: because he was a man of war, therefore he had Gilead and Bashan.
corruption_summary: A firstborn son whose whole record is family tenderness followed by armed conquest under divine grant does not fit a reading that treats the conquest narratives as later nationalist invention.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholarship that treats the conquest accounts of Numbers and Joshua as tribal-origin legends composed centuries after the fact to justify later land claims has to explain away the plain, unglamorous shape of Machir’s story — a named man, a named son, a named clan, a named territory taken by named force, all fitting exactly into the larger genealogical and geographical record of the Pentateuch and Joshua with no seam. The text does not read like propaganda manufactured to justify a later border; it reads like a family register that happens to include a war.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that inheritance in Scripture is never bare entitlement; Machir’s house received Gilead because Machir was “a man of war” who went up and took it under the LORD’s commission (Numbers 32), a pattern of active, laborious possession that stands against every therapeutic notion of inheritance as something owed without cost or obedience.
roots_summary: Hebrew Makir (H4353), from makar (H4376), to sell; Gil'ad (H1568), Gilead; bekor (H1060), firstborn; yarash (H3423), to take possession, dispossess.
roots_lines: Hebrew Makir (H4353) — from makar (H4376), to sell; by extension, acquired at a price.
Hebrew Gil'ad (H1568) — Gilead, the land Machir’s house both named and conquered.
Hebrew bekor (H1060) — firstborn; Machir’s standing as Manasseh’s firstborn.
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to take possession, to dispossess; the verb of Numbers 32:39.
Hebrew gibbor (H1368) — mighty man, man of war; Joshua’s description of Machir’s house.
usage: “The children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph's knees” — the tenderness that opens the record.
“Machir begat Gilead” — the man’s name becomes the land’s.
“Because he was a man of war, therefore he had Gilead and Bashan” — inheritance following labor.

pos: n. (the firstborn son of Abraham by Keturah)
etymology: Hebrew Zimran (H2175), possibly from zamar (H2167), to make music, sing praise; or related to a root meaning celebrated, or vine-dresser.
biblical_def: Zimran is named first among the six sons Abraham had by Keturah, the wife he took after Sarah’s death: “Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah. And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah” (Genesis 25:1–2). The same list is preserved word for word in the Chronicler’s genealogy generations later (1 Chronicles 1:32), a small but real witness to the care with which even Abraham’s non-covenant line was kept in Israel’s own historical memory. Scripture records nothing further of Zimran personally, but the pattern surrounding him is instructive: “unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country” (Genesis 25:6), while “Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac” (Genesis 25:5). Zimran and his brothers become, in later tradition, the eponymous heads of Arabian tribes east of Canaan — a real, numerous, and historically significant people, yet deliberately set outside the line of promise even as their father Abraham provided for them in this life.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Zimran; he is the firstborn of Abraham’s six sons by Keturah, sent eastward with gifts while Isaac alone received the inheritance of promise.
webster_full: ZIMRAN, n. The firstborn son of Abraham by Keturah, ancestor of an Arabian tribe east of Canaan.
CONCUBINE, n. In Scripture, a secondary wife, of inferior legal standing to the primary wife, but a true wife nonetheless.
COVENANT, n. An agreement; in theology, God's gracious compact with His people, established with Isaac and not with Abraham's other sons.
PROMISE, n. A declaration which gives to another a right to expect or claim the performance of some act.
GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of persons or families from an ancestor.
scriptures: Genesis 25:1
Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah.
Genesis 25:2
And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah.
Genesis 25:6
But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country.
1 Chronicles 1:32
Now the sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine: she bare Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah. And the sons of Jokshan; Sheba, and Dedan.
corruption_summary: A bare genealogical name, transmitted identically across two books written centuries apart, is exactly the sort of unglamorous detail a late, careless redaction of the Pentateuch is least able to account for.
corruption_paragraphs: The documentary hypothesis, which treats Genesis as a patchwork of sources stitched together long after the events, struggles to explain why a name with no narrative weight whatsoever — Zimran appears in a list and nowhere else — is preserved verbatim by the Chronicler writing after the exile. A tradition careless enough to invent sources would have far less reason to be this careful with a name that does nothing for the plot.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD’s own sovereign distinguishing between children of the same father: Zimran, though a true son of Abraham and provided for in temporal goods, stands outside the covenant line of promise reserved for Isaac — unconditional election operating even within one man’s own household, and operating before either child had done good or evil (Romans 9:11).
roots_summary: Hebrew Zimran (H2175), from zamar (H2167), to sing praise, make music; Qeturah (H6989), Keturah; pilegesh (H6370), concubine; mizrach (H4217), the east.
roots_lines: Hebrew Zimran (H2175) — possibly from zamar (H2167), to make music, sing praise.
Hebrew Qeturah (H6989) — Keturah, Abraham’s wife after Sarah’s death.
Hebrew pilegesh (H6370) — concubine; the Chronicler’s own word for Keturah’s standing.
Hebrew mizrach (H4217) — the east; the direction Abraham sent Zimran and his brothers.
Hebrew matanah (H4979) — gift; what Abraham gave the sons of the concubines.
usage: “She bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan” — the opening of Keturah’s line.
“Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away” — provision without inheritance.
“Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac” — the covenant line singled out.

pos: n. (the third son of Abraham by Keturah)
etymology: Hebrew Medan (H4091), of uncertain derivation, possibly related to a root meaning judgment or strife, and possibly a shortened form connected to Midian.
biblical_def: Medan stands third in the list of the six sons Abraham had by Keturah: “And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah” (Genesis 25:2), a list the Chronicler repeats without alteration a millennium later (1 Chronicles 1:32). The nearness of his name to his brother Midian’s — the two are sometimes thought to represent branches of a single tribal confederation — has led some to treat Medan as scarcely distinct from Midian, yet Scripture lists them as two separate sons of one mother, and the dictionary honors the text’s own count. As with his brothers, nothing further is recorded of Medan by name; he belongs to the general company of whom it is said Abraham “gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country” (Genesis 25:6), while the whole of Abraham’s covenant inheritance passed to Isaac alone (Genesis 25:5). Medan is thus a real, named, historical son of the father of the faithful, and at the same time a permanent witness that physical descent from Abraham was never itself the ground of the promise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Medan; he is the third of Abraham’s sons by Keturah, sent east with gifts while the covenant inheritance remained with Isaac alone.
webster_full: MEDAN, n. The third son of Abraham by Keturah, head of an Arabian tribal line east of Canaan.
KETURAH, n. The wife Abraham took after the death of Sarah, bearing him six sons.
ELECTION, n. In theology, God's eternal and sovereign choice of some to salvation, according to His own good pleasure.
DESCENT, n. The act of passing from an ancestor to an heir; lineage; extraction.
SOVEREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; in theology, God's absolute right to dispose of His creatures and His gifts as He wills.
scriptures: Genesis 25:2
And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah.
Genesis 25:1
Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah.
Genesis 25:6
But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country.
1 Chronicles 1:32
Now the sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine: she bare Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah. And the sons of Jokshan; Sheba, and Dedan.
corruption_summary: That the text carefully counts Medan as one son distinct from Midian, rather than collapsing the two, argues against a late editor loosely inventing tribal genealogies for political convenience.
corruption_paragraphs: Ancient Near Eastern comparative approaches that treat tribal genealogies like this one as retrojected political fictions, drawn up to explain later relations between Israel and her neighbors, have to reckon with the text’s own restraint: it would have been easier, not harder, for a late inventor to merge Medan into Midian rather than preserve them as two distinct, adjacent, easily-confused brothers. The specificity argues for a genuine memory being transmitted, not a convenient fiction being manufactured.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the same sovereign distinguishing seen throughout Abraham’s family: many were born to Abraham, but only one carried the promise, for “in Isaac shall thy seed be called” (Genesis 21:12) — a pattern the Apostle Paul draws directly into New Testament doctrine as proof that God’s election runs by promise, not by mere physical descent (Romans 9:6–8).
roots_summary: Hebrew Medan (H4091), of uncertain root, possibly connected to strife or judgment; Midyan (H4080), Midian; zera' (H2233), seed, offspring; bekorah (H1062), birthright.

Hebrew Midyan (H4080) — Midian, Medan’s neighboring brother in the list.
Hebrew zera' (H2233) — seed, offspring; the word at the heart of the promise to Isaac.
Hebrew bekorah (H1062) — birthright; what Isaac held and the sons of Keturah did not.
Hebrew matanah (H4979) — gift; the temporal portion Medan received in place of inheritance.
usage: “Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan” — the third son named in order.
“The sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine” — the Chronicler’s repeated register.
“Sent them away from Isaac his son” — the covenant line kept singular.

pos: n. (the fifth son of Abraham by Keturah)
etymology: Hebrew Yishbaq (H3435), possibly from a root meaning he leaves free, or he releases.
biblical_def: Ishbak is named fifth of the six sons born to Abraham by Keturah: “And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah” (Genesis 25:2), the list repeated exactly by the Chronicler generations afterward (1 Chronicles 1:32). His name, like several of his brothers’, has been connected by later students of the region to tribal or place names east of Canaan, though Scripture itself supplies no narrative for him beyond his birth and his place in the family register. What Scripture does supply is the disposition Abraham made of him and his brothers: “unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country” (Genesis 25:6). Abraham’s care for Ishbak — a real gift, given while the patriarch still lived, so that the matter could not be disputed after his death — stands beside the far greater fact that “Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac” (Genesis 25:5). Ishbak thus receives temporal provision from a father’s hand without receiving the covenant that made that father the father of the faithful.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Ishbak; he is the fifth of Abraham’s sons by Keturah, provided for with gifts and sent eastward while Isaac alone inherited the covenant.
webster_full: ISHBAK, n. The fifth son of Abraham by Keturah, sent eastward with a portion of goods in his father's lifetime.
PORTION, n. A part or share; that which is allotted or distributed to a particular person.
PATRIARCH, n. The father and ruler of a family; one of the progenitors of the Hebrew nation.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over His creatures.
BIRTHRIGHT, n. The right, privilege, or possession into which one is born; especially the rights of the firstborn.
scriptures: Genesis 25:2
And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah.
Genesis 25:6
But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country.
Genesis 25:5
And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac.
1 Chronicles 1:32
Now the sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine: she bare Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah. And the sons of Jokshan; Sheba, and Dedan.
corruption_summary: The deliberate, orderly distribution described here — gifts given, sons sent away, one heir left standing — reads as careful legal memory, not the vague folk-legend a late invented genealogy would produce.
corruption_paragraphs: Source-critical readings that assign the Genesis genealogies to a late, priestly hand assembling scattered traditions cannot easily explain why the account is this legally precise: gifts distributed while the patriarch still lived, so that no future claim could be made against the inheritance, is exactly the kind of concrete legal detail a folk legend has no motive to invent and every reason, if fabricating, to leave vague.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God’s common grace to those outside the covenant — Ishbak receives a real portion from a real father — is not itself saving grace; Abraham could give Ishbak goods, but only the LORD could give Isaac the promise, and no earthly inheritance substitutes for standing in the covenant of grace (Ephesians 2:12).

Hebrew mattanah (H4979) — gift; what Abraham gave Ishbak and his brothers.
Hebrew shalach (H7971) — to send away; the verb governing Abraham’s act.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — inheritance; what Ishbak did not receive, and Isaac alone did.
Hebrew mizrach (H4217) — the east; the direction of Ishbak’s sending.

“Sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived” — provision made final in Abraham’s lifetime.
“Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac” — the singular heir of the covenant.

pos: n. (the third and youngest daughter born to Job after his restoration)
etymology: Hebrew Qeren ha-Puk (H7163), literally "horn of eye-paint" or "horn of antimony," the vessel that held the dark cosmetic used to darken the eyelids.
biblical_def: Keren-happuch is the third daughter given to Job after the LORD turned his captivity and blessed his latter end more than his beginning (Job 42:12), named together with her sisters Jemima and Kezia: “And he called the name of the first, Jemima; and the name of the second, Kezia; and the name of the third, Kerenhappuch” (Job 42:14). Her name, meaning a horn or vessel of dark eye-cosmetic, was among the most beautifying ornaments known in the ancient Near East, and the text pointedly adds, “in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job” (Job 42:15). What makes her more than a note on ancient cosmetics is the clause that follows: “their father gave them inheritance among their brethren” (Job 42:15), an extraordinary act in a culture where daughters did not ordinarily share in the paternal inheritance alongside sons. Job, restored beyond all he had lost (Job 42:13, seven sons and three daughters again), used his restored wealth to honor his daughters in a manner Scripture elsewhere reserves for exceptional cases (compare the daughters of Zelophehad, Numbers 27), a father’s free and particular kindness rather than a claim of ordinary right.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Keren-happuch; her name means a horn of eye-paint, and she is the youngest and most beautiful of the three daughters given to Job after his restoration, granted an unusual inheritance among her brothers.
webster_full: KERENHAPPUCH, n. The third daughter born to Job after his restoration, whose name signifies a horn of cosmetic eye-paint.
RESTORATION, n. The act of restoring; renewal; return to a former, especially a better, state.
INHERITANCE, n. That which is or may be inherited; a possession received from an ancestor by right of birth or bequest.
COMELY, a. Pleasing or agreeable to the sight; graceful; handsome.
PATRIMONY, n. An estate inherited from one's father or ancestors.
scriptures: And he called the name of the first, Jemima; and the name of the second, Kezia; and the name of the third, Kerenhappuch.
And in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job: and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren.
He had also seven sons and three daughters.
So the LORD blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning: for he had fourteen thousand sheep, and six thousand camels, and a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses.
corruption_summary: A father freely honoring daughters with inheritance out of restored abundance is not evidence of proto-egalitarian gender theory; it is a particular grace within an unaltered patriarchal household.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readings eager to find biblical warrant for a general dissolution of male-headed inheritance customs seize on Job’s gift to his daughters as though it establishes a rule rather than records an exception. The text nowhere says daughters ordinarily inherited alongside sons in patriarchal Israel or the patriarchal age; it says this father, out of restored abundance and evident delight in his restored family, chose to honor his daughters beyond the custom — a free act of a household head, not the abolition of headship.

The therapeutic reading that fixates on the daughters’ beauty and inheritance as Job’s statement of “value” for women in the abstract misses the actual shape of the text: Job named his restored family, delighted in them, and provided for them richly, which is simply what a godly patriarch does for those under his care (1 Timothy 5:8), not a rebuke of male headship but an exercise of it in generous form.

pos: n. (a wife of Caleb the son of Hezron, of the tribe of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Yerioth (H3408), curtains, tent-curtains, plural of yeri'ah, a curtain such as those of the tabernacle.
biblical_def: Jerioth appears once, in the genealogy of Judah kept by the Chronicler: “And Caleb the son of Hezron begat children of Azubah his wife, and of Jerioth: her sons are these; Jesher, and Shobab, and Ardon” (1 Chronicles 2:18). She is named alongside Azubah as a wife (or, by some readings of the Hebrew, possibly as a further description of Azubah herself) of this Caleb son of Hezron, a Judahite genealogically distinct from the more famous Caleb the son of Jephunneh who spied out the land. Her name, meaning curtains, is the very word used throughout Exodus for the ten linen curtains of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:1), a striking word to carry as a personal name in a family that stood, generation by generation, in the tribal line from which the tabernacle’s own priesthood-adjacent leadership and later David’s throne would come. This Caleb’s house continues immediately in the record: after Azubah’s death he took Ephrath, who bare him Hur (1 Chronicles 2:19), the ancestor, several generations on, of Bethlehem (1 Chronicles 2:50–51) and so of the messianic line. Jerioth’s sons stand at the root of that same reckoned house.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Jerioth; her name means curtains, the same word used of the tabernacle hangings, and she is a wife of Caleb the son of Hezron in the Chronicler's genealogy of Judah.
webster_full: JERIOTH, n. A wife of Caleb the son of Hezron, of the tribe of Judah, named in the Chronicler's genealogy.
CURTAIN, n. A hanging cloth, used in Scripture especially of the linen and goats'-hair hangings of the tabernacle.
GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of persons or families from an ancestor.
TRIBE, n. A family, race, or series of generations descended from the same progenitor.
HEZRON, n. A son of Pharez, grandson of Judah, from whom descended the family of Caleb and, eventually, David.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 2:18
And Caleb the son of Hezron begat children of Azubah his wife, and of Jerioth: her sons are these; Jesher, and Shobab, and Ardon.
1 Chronicles 2:19
And when Azubah was dead, Caleb took unto him Ephrath, which bare him Hur.
1 Chronicles 2:9
The sons also of Hezron, that were born unto him; Jerahmeel, and Ram, and Chelubai.
1 Chronicles 2:50
These were the sons of Caleb the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah; Shobal the father of Kirjathjearim.
corruption_summary: A single-verse woman in a dense tribal genealogy, preserved without embellishment or legend, argues for a genuine archival source behind Chronicles, not late nationalist invention.
corruption_paragraphs: A minimalist historiography that treats the Chronicler’s genealogies as post-exilic legitimating fiction, composed to give the returned community a usable past, has to account for names like Jerioth — too minor, too textually difficult, and too narratively unrewarding to have been invented for propaganda. A forger inventing an ancestry does not bother with a nearly-anonymous second wife whose sons do nothing notable; a compiler working from real family records does.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD’s providence in the small links of a long chain: an obscure wife of an obscure Caleb, in an obscure verse, sits within the very tribal house from which Hur, Bethlehem, and ultimately David and Christ descend (1 Chronicles 2:50–51) — every generation matters to the God who counts them all.

Hebrew Chetsron (H2696) — Hezron, the father of Caleb and grandfather of Jerioth’s sons.
Hebrew Kalev (H3612) — Caleb, Jerioth’s husband, wholehearted or dog-like in devotion.
Hebrew toledoth (H8435) — generations; the Chronicler’s governing structure.
Hebrew ben (H1121) — son; the word introducing each name in the register.

“Her sons are these; Jesher, and Shobab, and Ardon” — the line she leaves behind.
“Caleb took unto him Ephrath, which bare him Hur” — the house continuing toward Bethlehem.

pos: n. (a false prophetess hired to intimidate Nehemiah)
etymology: Hebrew Noadyah (H5129), meaning "the LORD has met" or "the LORD has assembled," from ya'ad, to appoint, meet.
biblical_def: Noadiah is named by Nehemiah himself in prayer, among the enemies who tried to stop the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s wall: “My God, think thou upon Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works, and on the prophetess Noadiah, and the rest of the prophets, that would have put me in fear” (Nehemiah 6:14). The immediate context names a hired accomplice, Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, who pretended a message from God urging Nehemiah to hide in the temple as though his life were in danger — “therefore was he hired, that I should be afraid, and do so, and sin” (Nehemiah 6:13). Nehemiah, discerning the counterfeit, refused: “Should such a man as I flee? and who is there, that, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life? I will not go in” (Nehemiah 6:11). Noadiah is grouped with this whole company of false prophets hired by Sanballat and Tobiah to work on Nehemiah’s fear rather than his faith, and her title “the prophetess” is Scripture’s own word for her claimed office — a claim the text records without endorsing, precisely as it names Tobiah and Sanballat without endorsing them. She is a rare biblical instance of a woman explicitly identified as a false prophet by name, standing in stark contrast to true prophetesses such as Deborah, Huldah, and Miriam.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Noadiah; she is a false prophetess named by Nehemiah among those hired to intimidate him from finishing the wall of Jerusalem.
webster_full: NOADIAH, n. A false prophetess who conspired with Sanballat and Tobiah to frighten Nehemiah from his work.
PROPHETESS, n. A female prophet; a woman who claims or exercises the office of speaking for God.
FALSE PROPHET, n. One who falsely claims divine inspiration or falsely speaks in the name of the LORD.
INTIMIDATE, v.t. To make fearful; to inspire with fear by threats or violence.
DISCERNMENT, n. The power or faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes one thing from another; judgment.
scriptures: Nehemiah 6:14
My God, think thou upon Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works, and on the prophetess Noadiah, and the rest of the prophets, that would have put me in fear.
Nehemiah 6:13
Therefore was he hired, that I should be afraid, and do so, and sin, and that they might have matter for an evil report, that they might reproach me.
Nehemiah 6:11
And I said, Should such a man as I flee? and who is there, that, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life? I will not go in.
Nehemiah 6:10

Afterward I came unto the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah the son of Mehetabeel, who was shut up; and he said, Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple, and let us shut the doors of the temple: for they will come to slay thee; yea, in the night will they come to slay thee.
corruption_summary: Naming a female opponent by title and name, without softening her as merely misguided, is precisely the kind of unflattering historical particularity a self-serving national memoir would omit.
corruption_paragraphs: Progressive readings that treat every biblical woman exercising a spiritual title as evidence of Scripture's approval of that exercise cannot be applied uniformly to Noadiah, whose title of prophetess is recorded by the very man she opposed, in a prayer asking God to remember her deeds against her. The text distinguishes carefully between an office claimed and an office validated; only the latter carries Scripture’s endorsement, and Noadiah plainly lacks it.

Modern conflict-resolution instincts that would soften Nehemiah’s naming of Noadiah as harsh or unforgiving miss that this is inspired prayer, not personal grievance — the psalmists pray the same way against the wicked (Psalm 69, Psalm 109), and Nehemiah’s petition that God remember her works is an appeal to the LORD’s own justice against those who would have derailed His work through manufactured fear and false claims to divine speech, a sin the law itself treats with the utmost seriousness (Deuteronomy 18:20).
roots_summary: Hebrew Noadyah (H5129), from ya'ad (H3259), to appoint, meet; nabiy'ah (H5031), prophetess; sheqer (H8267), falsehood, a lie; yare' (H3372), to fear.
roots_lines: Hebrew Noadyah (H5129) — the LORD has met, or has assembled; from ya'ad, to appoint.
Hebrew nabiy'ah (H5031) — prophetess; the title Nehemiah records without endorsing.
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; the character of the message Shemaiah brought.
Hebrew yare' (H3372) — to fear; the response the conspirators sought to provoke in Nehemiah.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember; the verb of Nehemiah’s prayer against her.
usage: “The prophetess Noadiah, and the rest of the prophets” — grouped with the hired opposition.
“That would have put me in fear” — the aim of the whole scheme.
“Should such a man as I flee?” — Nehemiah’s discerning refusal.

pos: n. (the ancient name of Hebron, before Israel's conquest)
etymology: Hebrew Qiryath Arba' (H7153), "city of Arba," from qiryah, city, and Arba', the name of the great man among the Anakims for whom it was called.
biblical_def: Kirjath-arba is Scripture’s own name for Hebron before the conquest, and the text repeatedly stops to make the identification explicit rather than leave it assumed: “Sarah died in Kirjatharba; the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan” (Genesis 23:2); “the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba” (Joshua 14:15); “the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba” again (Judges 1:10). The name means “city of Arba,” for “Arba was a great man among the Anakims” (Joshua 14:15) — one of the giant-statured peoples whose report had terrified the ten faithless spies a generation earlier (Numbers 13:33). That this city of giants became, by God’s own appointment, the burial place of Sarah, the inheritance of faithful Caleb, and eventually the first capital of David’s kingdom (2 Samuel 5:5), is one of the plainer pictures in the historical books of faith inheriting what fear once refused. Judah’s conquest of it is recorded plainly: “Judah went against the Canaanites that dwelt in Hebron... and they slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai” (Judges 1:10), the same three sons of Anak Caleb had asked for by name (Joshua 15:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Kirjath-arba; it is the ancient, pre-conquest name of Hebron, meaning city of Arba, a great man among the giant Anakims.
webster_full: KIRJATH-ARBA, n. The ancient name of Hebron, meaning the city of Arba, a chief man among the Anakim giants.
HEBRON, n. An ancient city of Judah, given to Caleb, and later the first capital of King David.
ANAKIM, n. A race of giants inhabiting Canaan before the conquest, feared by the ten faithless spies.
GIANT, n. A man of extraordinary bulk and stature, above the ordinary size of men.
CONQUEST, n. The act of overcoming and subduing by force; acquisition by war.
scriptures: Genesis 23:2
And Sarah died in Kirjatharba; the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan: and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.
Joshua 14:15
And the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba; which Arba was a great man among the Anakims. And the land had rest from war.
Judges 1:10
And Judah went against the Canaanites that dwelt in Hebron: (now the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba:) and they slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai.
Joshua 15:13
And unto Caleb the son of Jephunneh he gave a part among the children of Judah, according to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, even the city of Arba the father of Anak, which city is Hebron.
corruption_summary: The text's own repeated insistence on the old name behind the new one is the opposite of what a legend-building later editor would do, who has every motive to erase an embarrassing pagan-giant history, not preserve it three times over.
corruption_paragraphs: A skeptical historiography that treats the conquest narratives as later Israelite self-flattery cannot easily explain why the text goes out of its way, three separate times in three separate books, to remind the reader that the holy city of the patriarchs and of David was once named for a giant. A fabricated national epic minimizes inconvenient pagan pasts; Scripture instead advertises this one, because the point is not Israel’s greatness but the LORD’s power to give His people cities they did not build and did not fear to take by faith (Deuteronomy 6:10–11).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the same ground which broke the faith of ten spies (Numbers 13:33, “we were in our own sight as grasshoppers”) became, one generation later, the inheritance of the two who believed, Caleb and Joshua — unbelief sees giants and retreats; faith sees the same giants and asks for the mountain (Joshua 14:12).
roots_summary: Hebrew Qiryah (H7151), city; Arba' (H704), Arba, four; Anaqim (H6062), the Anakim giants; nachalah (H5159), inheritance.
roots_lines: Hebrew qiryah (H7151) — city; the first element of the ancient name.
Hebrew Arba' (H704) — Arba, possibly meaning four; the great man for whom the city was named.
Hebrew Anaqim (H6062) — the Anakim; the giant clan of which Arba was a chief.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — inheritance; what the city became for Caleb by faith.
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to take possession, dispossess; the verb of Judah’s conquest.
usage: “Sarah died in Kirjatharba; the same is Hebron” — the identification made at the patriarchal age.
“The name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba” — repeated at the conquest.
“Arba was a great man among the Anakims” — the giant behind the ancient name.

pos: n. (the ancient clan-name and district of Bethlehem, and the prophesied birthplace of the Messiah)
etymology: Hebrew Ephrathah (H672), possibly meaning "fruitful," related to parah, to bear fruit; the older name of the clan and region later called Bethlehem.
biblical_def: Ephrathah is the older name attached to the district and clan out of which Bethlehem grew, most memorably fixed in the burial notice for Rachel: “Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem” (Genesis 35:19), the same explanatory formula Scripture uses elsewhere to identify Kirjath-arba as Hebron. The Chronicler traces the name to a person as well as a place, naming Ephrath as wife of Caleb and mother of Hur (1 Chronicles 2:19), whose own descendants are called “the sons of Caleb the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah” (1 Chronicles 2:50) — the district evidently taking, or giving, its name within this same Judahite family line. The name reaches its highest use in Micah’s messianic prophecy, where the double name is deliberately joined: “thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” (Micah 5:2). And at the threshold of the book of Ruth, the same name is invoked as a blessing on the house of Boaz: “do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem” (Ruth 4:11), a blessing fulfilled beyond the elders’ own imagining in the line that ran from Boaz through David to Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Ephrathah; it is the ancient clan-name and district identified with Bethlehem, joined to it by name in Micah's prophecy of the Messiah's birthplace.
webster_full: EPHRATHAH, n. The ancient name of the district and clan out of which Bethlehem arose, joined with Bethlehem in Micah's messianic prophecy.
BETHLEHEM, n. A small town of Judah, the birthplace of David and, in fulfillment of prophecy, of Jesus Christ.
PROPHECY, n. A declaration of something to come, made under divine inspiration.
MESSIAH, n. The Anointed One; the Christ promised throughout the Old Testament and fulfilled in Jesus.
EVERLASTING, a. Lasting or enduring forever; eternal; without beginning or end, applied properly to God alone.
scriptures: Genesis 35:19
And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.
Micah 5:2

But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
Ruth 4:11

And all the people that were in the gate, and the elders, said, We are witnesses. The LORD make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel: and do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem:
1 Chronicles 2:19
And when Azubah was dead, Caleb took unto him Ephrath, which bare him Hur.
corruption_summary: A prophecy naming an obscure double place-name centuries in advance, fulfilled to the letter in a village too small to be politically significant, resists every attempt to read Micah 5:2 as vague or after-the-fact.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholarship eager to date Micah's prophecy after the event, or to read it as generalized royal-court flattery rather than specific prediction, cannot account for the deliberate smallness of the claim: “though thou be little among the thousands of Judah” is not the language a court poet uses to flatter a reigning king's birthplace after the fact; it is the language of a specific, humble, verifiable prediction later fulfilled exactly, down to the double ancient name, in the birth recorded in Matthew 2:5–6.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God fixes His greatest works in the smallest, most overlooked places — Ephrathah, a clan-district too minor to need its name explained except by cross-reference to a more famous town, is the LORD's own chosen cradle for the everlasting Ruler, confounding every merely human calculation of where glory ought to be found (1 Corinthians 1:27–28).
roots_summary: Hebrew Ephrathah (H672), from parah (H6509), to bear fruit; Beyth Lechem (H1035), house of bread; yatsa' (H3318), to go forth, come out; moshel (H4910), ruler.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ephrathah (H672) — possibly fruitful, from parah, to bear fruit.
Hebrew Beyth Lechem (H1035) — house of bread; the town Ephrathah is identified with.
Hebrew yatsa' (H3318) — to go forth, come out; the verb of Micah’s prophecy.
Hebrew moshel (H4910) — ruler, one who has dominion; the office of the promised child.
Hebrew olam (H5769) — forever, everlasting; the age from which His goings forth have been.
usage: “Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem” — the ancient identification.
“Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little” — the prophecy of the Messiah’s birthplace.
“Do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem” — the elders’ blessing on Boaz.

pos: n. (the combined Median-Persian empire of Daniel's prophecy, successor to Babylon)
etymology: A compound of Media and Persia, the two allied kingdoms whose combined empire, under Cyrus, overthrew Babylon and is named jointly throughout Daniel and Esther.
biblical_def: Medo-Persia is Scripture’s own compound reckoning of the empire that conquered Babylon and ruled the known world through the era of Daniel, Esther, Ezra, and Nehemiah — named jointly, and in that fixed order, again and again rather than treated as Persia alone. The handwriting on Belshazzar’s wall pronounces the verdict in these very terms: “PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians” (Daniel 5:28), fulfilled that same night. Daniel’s vision of the ram with two horns is interpreted explicitly: “The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia” (Daniel 8:20), the second, higher horn representing Persia’s eventual dominance within the alliance. The empire’s legal character — a fixed, unchangeable law, distinct from the personal despotism of Babylon — is twice made a matter of high drama: “the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” traps Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6:8), and the same irrevocable “law of the Persians and the Medes” is invoked to seal Vashti’s deposing in Esther 1:19. This dual empire is the silver kingdom of Nebuchadnezzar’s image (Daniel 2:39) and the bear of Daniel’s vision (Daniel 7:5), inferior to Babylon’s gold yet the LORD’s own appointed instrument to end the captivity and send Cyrus to rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1–2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry under this compound form; Medo-Persia is the joint Median-Persian empire of Daniel's prophecies, whose fixed, unalterable law and eventual overthrow of Babylon are recorded across Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther.
webster_full: MEDO-PERSIA, n. The combined empire of the Medes and Persians, successor to Babylon, prominent in the prophecies of Daniel.
PERSIA, n. An ancient empire of southwestern Asia, whose kings, beginning with Cyrus, permitted the Jews' return from captivity.
MEDE, n. A native or inhabitant of Media, an ancient country allied with, and eventually absorbed into, the Persian empire.
IRREVOCABLE, a. Incapable of being recalled, revoked, or annulled; unalterable.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over His creatures, directing even the decrees of pagan empires.
scriptures: Daniel 5:28
PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.
Daniel 8:20
The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia.
Daniel 6:8
Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not.
Esther 1:19

If it please the king, let there go a royal commandment from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered, That Vashti come no more before king Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal estate unto another that is better than she.
corruption_summary: Prophecy naming, in advance, a specific two-part empire with a legal character unlike its predecessor's and its consequent overthrow of Babylon is a poor fit for a book critics insist was written after the fact.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholarship that dates the book of Daniel to the second century BC, precisely to explain away its apparent foreknowledge of Medo-Persia's rise and fall, still cannot account for the accuracy of secondary details embedded incidentally in the narrative — the peculiar, historically attested fact of an unalterable royal law unique to this empire (Daniel 6:8; Esther 1:19) is exactly the kind of texture a writer working centuries after the fact, from garbled memory, would be unlikely to preserve so precisely.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Daniel's own doxology upon receiving these very visions: “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Daniel 2:21). Medo-Persia's rise to overthrow Babylon and its own later fall to Greece were not accidents of history but the LORD's own ordering of Gentile empires toward the fixed goal of Christ's kingdom, which alone “shall never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44).
roots_summary: Hebrew/Aramaic Maday (H4074), Media; Paras (H6539), Persia; malkuth (H4437), kingdom; shena' (H8133), to change, alter.
roots_lines: Aramaic Maday (H4074) — Media; the first element of the compound name.
Aramaic Paras (H6539) — Persia; the second, and eventually dominant, element.
Aramaic malkuth (H4437) — kingdom; the word of Daniel 5:28's pronouncement.
Aramaic shena' (H8133) — to change, alter; the very thing the Medo-Persian law could not do.
Hebrew dath (H1881) — law, decree; the fixed legal character of the empire in Esther and Daniel.
usage: “Given to the Medes and Persians” — the verdict of the handwriting on the wall.
“The kings of Media and Persia” — Gabriel's interpretation of the two-horned ram.
“The law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” — the empire's fixed legal character.
